notes:
These notes on Psalm 139 go verse by verse. Each point names its source and gives the page URL. The most-used pages are Enduring Word (David Guzik), Spurgeon's *Treasury of David*, the Pulpit Commentary, Matthew Henry, and the verse-by-verse pages on StudyLight. Verses where I found little are kept short.

**Gaps:** My searches turned up nothing on Psalm 139 from Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), Wesley's own notes, catholic.com, bibleodyssey.org, or prosperity / word-of-faith / hyper-grace teaching, so none of those appear below. Augustine's exposition (newadvent.org) cut off at verse 12, so I only have his reading of verses 1–12.

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik: David is praying to Yahweh, who knows him personally. Pagans often thought their gods were hostile or indifferent, but David knew the true God cares enough to search and know each person.  (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-139/)
- Spurgeon: "searching" usually implies some ignorance that observation removes. That isn't so with God; the point is that He knows us as thoroughly as if He had examined every corner.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps139.cfm)
- Pulpit Commentary: the sense is "searched me out," meaning God has looked into all my thoughts and feelings and fully knows my spiritual condition.  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/139.htm)
- Bible.org (Utley): "know" here means intimate, personal knowledge.  (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-139)
- **Catholic reading (Augustine):** he reads the psalm as Christ speaking, sometimes for Himself and sometimes for His people, because He has made Himself one with them.  So "You have searched me" is Christ addressing the Father.  (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801139.htm)

**v. 2**
- Guzik: "sitting and rising" is a common phrase meaning God knows everything about David, even ordinary things. He links it to Matthew 10:30, where God numbers the hairs of our head.  (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-139/)
- Pulpit Commentary: "thoughts from afar" means God understands a thought while it is still forming, before it is fully developed.  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/139.htm)
- Charnock, quoted by Spurgeon: God's knowledge reaches thoughts at their source, before they are even ours.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps139.cfm)
- Adam Clarke (Methodist): even small, passing actions like taking or leaving a seat are under God's constant notice.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/139-2.html)
- **Catholic reading (Augustine):** "sitting" is Christ humbled in His Passion and "rising" is His Resurrection. For believers, a person "sits" in humble repentance and "rises" when forgiven.  He also links "from afar" to the prodigal son, whose father knew his thoughts while he was still far away.  (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801139.htm)

**v. 3**
- Pulpit Commentary: the verb is better read "siftest." "Path and lying down" means the times of activity and of rest.  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/139.htm)
- Spurgeon: the Hebrew means winnowing and sifting, not just surrounding. God separates the good from the evil in both our work and our rest.  This should make us careful not to sin, brave so we don't fear, and glad so we don't mourn.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps139.cfm)
- **Catholic reading (Augustine):** "my path" is the wrong road the sinner took away from the Father. God saw it in advance and let the wanderer toil so he might come back.  (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801139.htm)

**v. 4**
- Calvin (Reformed): the words can be read two ways. Either God knows what we will say before we say it, or God knows our hidden intentions even when we keep silent. Calvin says it doesn't matter which, because both mean the same thing.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/139-4.html)
- Clarke (Methodist): God knows our words before they are spoken, just as He knows our thoughts before they are formed.  (same URL)
- Matthew Henry: God knows what each word meant, which thought it came from, and why it was said.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_139.cfm)
- Guzik applies this to speech: Christians who use profane or impure language should remember that God hears every word.  (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-139/)
- **Modern scholarship (Utley):** the ancient translations read this verse about evil speech. The Peshitta has "deception" and the Septuagint has "unrighteous word."  (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-139)

**v. 5**
- Calvin: some read "fashioned me" here, but the Hebrew word often means "shut up." David means he is surrounded on every side and cannot escape.  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/139.htm)
- Pulpit Commentary: God knows everything about him because He is always close to him. His hand is there both to hold him up and to hold him back.  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/139.htm)
- Matthew Henry suggests the picture may be a doctor laying his hand on a patient to feel the pulse.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_139.cfm)
- Spurgeon: God is behind us, recording our sins or, in grace, blotting them out. He is before us, knowing our deeds in advance and providing for our needs.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps139.cfm)
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel): looking back he sees God's hand on his life, looking ahead he sees God's plan, and right now he feels God's hand on him.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/139-13.html)

**v. 6**
- Guzik: David saw that God knew him better than he knew himself, and that is a humbling place to be.  (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-139/)
- Matthew Henry: God knows me in a way I don't and can't know myself.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_139.cfm)
- David Dickson, quoted by Spurgeon: when we look at God's perfections we should notice our own imperfections and search into God more modestly.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps139.cfm)
- Utley: in the end we have to trust God without fully understanding Him.  (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-139)

**v. 7**
- A writer quoted by Spurgeon: "Spirit" here means God's understanding and knowledge, not just His power, and "presence" (literally "face") means His watching eye.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps139.cfm)
- Another quotation in Spurgeon distinguishes the ways God is present: His glory in heaven, His power on earth, His justice in hell, and His grace with His people.  (same URL)
- Guzik quotes a commentator: God is everywhere, yet He is not everything. He is present in creation but distinct from it.  (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-139/)
- Barnes (Presbyterian): those who hate God can never find a place where a holy God is absent, which is a fearful thought for them.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-139.html)
- **Catholic reading (Augustine):** the person running away cannot escape the eyes of the God he flees. He cites Wisdom 1:7, that the Spirit fills the world.  (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801139.htm)

**v. 8**
- A quotation in Spurgeon: "You are there" is not about God's knowledge, which was already covered in verses 2–3. It means God Himself, His very being, is there.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps139.cfm)
- Guzik: heaven is not too high and hell is not too low; God is everywhere.  (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-139/)
- **Catholic reading (Augustine):** if a person sinks into the depths of sin and refuses to confess, God is there too, to punish.  (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801139.htm)

**v. 9**
- Barnes: "the farthest sea" means the west, since the Mediterranean lay west of Israel. Even if he could fly as fast as light, God would already be there.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-139.html)
- **Catholic reading (Augustine):** "the farthest parts of the sea" is the end of the world. Believers should flee there in hope, on the "wings of twofold love."  (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801139.htm)

**v. 10**
- Calvin: "hand" means power. God could easily stop anyone trying to escape Him and bring them back.  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/139.htm)
- Spurgeon: the missionary exploring alone is led, and in his weakness he is held.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps139.cfm)
- **Catholic reading (Augustine):** the very God whose angry face we try to flee is the one who leads us home. We lost our wings through lust, Christ redeemed us with His blood, and we have free will but can do nothing unless He helps.  (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801139.htm)

**vv. 11–12**
- Barnes: darkness makes things dark to us, not to God. That is true of physical darkness and of moral darkness. He applies it to troubles: disappointment and loss look dark to us, but all is light to God.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-139.html)
- Spurgeon: people still choose darkness for their evil deeds, but nothing is hidden from God, so they might as well sin in broad daylight.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps139.cfm)
- **Catholic reading (Augustine):** the night was made light because Christ came down into it.  Sinners who defend their sin instead of confessing it "darken their darkness."  (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801139.htm)

**v. 13**
- Calvin: we shouldn't be surprised that God knows our most secret thoughts, since He formed our hearts and "reins." He pictures God as a king seated in the very depths of a person.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/139-13.html)
- Barnes: the verb means "made" or "created," not "possessed." "Reins" (literally kidneys) stand for the inner self, the seat of desires and feelings. The second verb means "wove" or "knit together."  (same URL)
- Clarke: the Hebrews believed the reins were the first part of a baby to form, so this may mean "you laid the foundation of my being."  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/139-13.html)
- Gill (Baptist): "covered me" means God wrapped him in the womb or clothed his bones with flesh, a sign of His care for him as an embryo.  (same URL)
- **Catholic reading (Augustine):** God "possesses" not only the heart (the thoughts) but the reins (the delights).  (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801139.htm)

**v. 14**
- Pulpit Commentary: praise has been running underneath the whole poem, and here it comes out openly.  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/139.htm)
- A note in Calvin's commentary: we are so "fearfully" made that almost any movement seems to risk some muscle or vein whose rupture would harm life or health.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/139-13.html)
- Calvin: the right way to look at God's works is the way that ends in wonder. The "knowing" in this verse is reverent attention that leads to thanks, not a claim to explain every mystery.  (same URL)
- Spurgeon: we don't need to travel to the ends of the earth for marvels; they are in our own bodies.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps139.cfm)

**v. 15**
- Coffman, citing Kidner: "the depths of the earth" is a picture of deep hiddenness, meaning the womb, with no mythological meaning. "Woven" suggests the complex work of a weaver or embroiderer.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/139-13.html)
- A quotation in Spurgeon: few places are more hidden than an unborn baby's, yet the psalmist pictures God present even there.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps139.cfm)

**v. 16**
- Guzik: God saw what no one else could see. His knowledge reached into David's future too, as if David's days were already written in a book.  (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-139/)
- Spurgeon: like an architect drawing up plans, God wrote down all our members in the book of His purposes.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps139.cfm)
- Barnes: while he was still an embryo, his whole future was known to God and written down: his form, how long he would live, and the events of his life.  (https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/lit/psalms/139-16.html)
- **Modern scholarship (NET Bible notes):** the Hebrew word for "unformed body," *golem*, appears only here in the Old Testament. In later Hebrew it meant a shapeless lump or unfinished vessel. The "scroll" may be the "scroll of life" of Psalm 69:28.  (https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=psa&chapter=139&verse=16)
- **Sanctity of life:** Guzik says God's concern for human life starts at conception.  (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-139/) The Bible Hub study notes say this matches the biblical view that life begins at conception.  (https://biblehub.com/study/psalms/139-16.htm)
- **Where views differ (God's plan vs. human freedom):** I did not find Calvinist and Arminian teachers directly arguing over this verse. What I found:
  - The Bible Hub study notes give a strongly providential reading: "written" implies a plan set in advance, so nothing in life is random or outside God's will.  (https://biblehub.com/study/psalms/139-16.htm)
  - Coffman (Churches of Christ) quotes a warning that rigid fatalism which removes human responsibility is unbiblical. He argues God's knowing tomorrow no more causes it than our knowing yesterday caused it.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/139-13.html)
  - A Bible Hub Q&A says the verse is poetry that affirms God's providence but is not a treatise on determinism. It notes that Augustine and the Reformers both kept God's ordering of all things together with a real human will.  (https://biblehub.com/q/Is_every_life_detail_predestined_by_God.htm)

**v. 17**
- Calvin: the Hebrew word means "thoughts," as in verse 2. It does not mean "companions" or "friends," as some have translated it following the Aramaic.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/139-17.html)
- Matthew Henry: God's thoughts toward him were loving, "of good, and not of evil" (Jeremiah 29:11). God's all-seeing knowledge could rightly have watched us to harm us, but it has watched over us for our good.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_139.cfm)
- Clarke: the word "sum" may also hint at "bones" (*atsamoth*).  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/139-17.html)
- Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik: David isn't alarmed that God knows everything about him; he feels comforted and enriched by it.  (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-139/)

**v. 18**
- Spurgeon: God's loving thoughts are beyond counting, and trying to count them would never end.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps139.cfm)
- Pulpit Commentary: "when I awake" means he thinks on God asleep and awake and never runs out of things to think about.  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/139.htm)
- Clarke: all his steps are ordered by God, and he is always under the Spirit's influence.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/139-18.html)

**v. 19**
- Matthew Henry: because God knows all the wickedness of the wicked, He will judge it. He may let them prosper for a while, but in the end He will slay them.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/139-18.html)
- Spurgeon: the God who sees all evil will slay all evil.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps139.cfm)
- Constable: David is praying against enemies who were trying to kill him.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/139-22.html)
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary suggests God may slay the wicked by slaying their wickedness, since you destroy an enemy by making him a friend.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/139-4.html)

**v. 20**
- Barnes: when people blaspheme or slander God's name, that is reason enough to avoid their company and friendship.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-139.html)
- Matthew Henry: people show their hostility by treating God's name as a joke, and anyone who uses the forms of oaths or prayer irreverently takes it in vain.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/139-22.html)

**vv. 21–22 ("perfect hatred")** This is the verse pair where readings differ most.
- **Baptist:**
  - Spurgeon: David was a "good hater" who hated only those who hated good. We should love all people with goodwill, but loving a wicked person "with complacency" (approval) would be a crime.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps139.cfm)
  - Gill: he hates them sincerely, in deed and not just in words. God's friends were David's friends and God's enemies were his.  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/139-22.htm)
  - A quotation in Spurgeon: the word "grieved" explains "hate." It is not hatred full of ill will but one that comes with grief and pity.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps139.cfm)
  - Spurgeon's collection also gives the classic definition: hate their sins, love them as God's creatures, and neither hate the people for their vices nor love the vices for the people's sake.  (same URL)
- **Reformed / Presbyterian:**
  - Calvin: anyone who goes along with sin by staying silent betrays God's cause.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/139-22.html)
  - Barnes: "perfect hatred" means complete disapproval of their conduct and no sympathy for their wrongdoing.  (same URL)
  - W. Robert Godfrey (Ligonier): we must not call down curses on people out of personal spite. But it is legitimate to pray for judgment on God's enemies, and praying "Come quickly, Lord Jesus" already does that.  (https://learn.ligonier.org/qas/how-should-christians-respond-to-imprecatory-psalms)
- **Methodist / Wesleyan:**
  - Clarke: what he abhors is their conduct, motives, opposition to God and idolatrous aims, and he will have no part with them.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/139-22.html)
- **Charismatic:**
  - Sam Storms: these prayers assume the wicked are hardened and unrepentant, and ask for judgment only *as long as* they keep rebelling. We love our enemies by praying for them to repent.  David knew he needed protection from hating God's enemies for personal reasons.  (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/imprecations-in-the-psalms-; https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/article-10-things-you-should-know-about-the-imprecatory-psalms)
- **Older Anglican-era view:**
  - The Pulpit Commentary says David regards them as his own personal enemies, and notes that the command "Love your enemies" had not yet been given.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/139-22.html)
  - Storms quotes the Pulpit Commentary elsewhere as calling such psalms "man's defective prayers" rather than God's commands.  (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/imprecations-in-the-psalms-)
  - Storms also quotes Halley's Handbook as calling them the opposite of Jesus' teaching.  (same URL)
- **Orthodox:**
  - Fr. Lawrence Farley (OCA) responds to a writer who called David's words here "the sinful voice of a human."  Farley says that writer never asked what "hate" means in this verse. Christ forbids revenge against personal enemies, whom we should pray for.  He urges believers to imitate this "holy hatred" by firmly rejecting wickedness.  (https://www.oca.org/reflections/fr.-lawrence-farley/holy-hatred)

**v. 23**
- Guzik: David brings his understanding of God's nature into his own discipleship; God's attributes are guides to growth, not mere theory.  (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-139/)
- Barnes: "try me" means test me the way metal is tested to show what it really is.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-139.html)
- Clarkson, quoted by Spurgeon: real faith is like gold and survives testing, while presumption is a counterfeit that can't.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps139.cfm)
- **A difference of emphasis:**
  - Matthew Henry and the Homiletical Commentary stress the honest person's confidence: those who are upright can calmly invite God to search them.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_139.cfm) and  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/139-22.html)
  - The same Homiletical Commentary also says a real Christian's heart can hide much undetected evil.  (same URL)
  - Chuck Smith reads it as an admission that we don't know our own hearts, and says the Holy Spirit's work includes showing us the truth about ourselves.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/139-13.html)

**v. 24**
- Matthew Henry: an honest man would like a window in his chest so anyone could see his heart. The prayer means: show me any corrupt leaning that remains and root it out.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/139-18.html)
- Guzik: "the way everlasting" is David's destination. The way of holiness he prayed for is the way that leads to everlasting life.  (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-139/)
- Storms links verses 23–24 back to verses 19–22: David asks God to purify his motives so his zeal doesn't turn into personal hatred.  (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/imprecations-in-the-psalms-)
- Fr. Farley (OCA) likewise says such wicked ways may hide in our own hearts, and we should pray for God to search us and root them out.  (https://www.oca.org/reflections/fr.-lawrence-farley/holy-hatred)
